<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract.</h6>
    <span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>School of Informatics</span></span></span>
    <span id="footnotex2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>Key Laboratory of Digital Protection and Intelligent Processing of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Fujian and Taiwan,Ministry of Culture and Tourism</span></span></span>
    <span id="footnotex3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>Institute of Artificial Intelligence</span></span></span>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become an essential method for mitigating hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) by leveraging external knowledge. Although effective for simple queries, traditional RAG struggles with large-scale, unstructured corpora where information is highly fragmented. Graph-based RAG (GraphRAG) incorporates knowledge graphs to capture structural relationships, enabling more comprehensive retrieval for complex reasoning. However, existing GraphRAG methods rely on isolated, fragment-level extraction for graph construction, lacking a global perspective on the whole corpus. As a result, these methods frequently lead to thematically inconsistent, logically conflicting, and structurally fragmented graphs that degrade retrieval performance. In this paper, we propose MemGraphRAG, a novel framework that introduces a memory-based multi-agent system to ensure high-quality graph construction. Specifically, MemGraphRAG employs a collaborative society of agents supported by shared memory, which provides a unified global context throughout the extraction process. This mechanism allows agents to dynamically resolve logical conflicts and maintain structural connectivity throughout the corpus. Furthermore, we propose a memory-aware hierarchical retrieval algorithm tailored for the constructed graph. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that MemGraphRAG outperforms the state-of-the-art baseline models with comparable efficiency. Our code is available at <a href="https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/MemGraphRAG" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/MemGraphRAG</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>RAG, GraphRAG, Multi Agent, Agent Memory, Indexing Graph 
</div><span id="id19" class="ltx_note ltx_role_cc-license"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">cc-license: </span>by</span></span></span>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.00610v1/intro.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/138;" width="229" height="138" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>. </span><span id="S0.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison between existing GraphRAG and MemGraphRAG. Exiting GraphRAG performs isolated chunk-level extraction without the global view, resulting in a noisy and inconsistent indexing graph. While MemGraphRAG incorporates global memory to ensure global consistency.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1. </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) effectively extends the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by leveraging external knowledge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lewis et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025c</a>)</cite>. However, existing RAG systems suffer from critical challenges in real-world scenarios. This is due to the unstructured and heterogeneous nature of large-scale corpora, where relevant information is often sparsely distributed. The contexts retrieved by RAG systems are often noisy and lack structural coherence. Although recent methods attempt to segment documents into smaller chunks for efficient indexing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Borgeaud et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Izacard et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, this strategy disrupts long-range dependencies and loses critical contextual details. As a result, the retrieved contexts are often incoherent or insufficient for complex reasoning tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address these limitations, Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Procko and Ochoa, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> has emerged as a powerful paradigm, leveraging external structured graphs to model the hierarchical structure of background knowledge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Early efforts, such as RAPTOR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sarthi et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and Microsoft’s GraphRAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Edge et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, organize knowledge through recursive summarization and community-level abstractions to support coarse-to-fine retrieval, thereby facilitating comprehensive response generation.
Subsequent methods, including GFM-RAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, G-Retriever <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and LightRAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, further incorporate specialized retrieval mechanisms and learning objectives to improve multi-hop generalization, scalability, and efficiency.
Most recently, HippoRAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gutiérrez et al., 2024</a>)</cite>and its enhancement HippoRAG2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gutiérrez et al., 2025</a>)</cite> have drawn inspiration from cognitive associative memory, utilizing algorithms such as Personalized PageRank to simulate multi-hop reasoning pathways.
These strategies demonstrate the potential of graph-baed retrieval in addressing the core limitations of traditional RAG.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S1.F2.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2606.00610v1/pre1.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/367;" width="476" height="367" alt="Refer to caption">
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S1.F2.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2606.00610v1/pre2.png" id="S1.F2.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/352;" width="476" height="352" alt="Refer to caption">
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>. </span><span id="S1.F2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">(Left)<span id="S1.F2.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Evaluation of representative RAG and GraphRAG systems. The radius reflecting performance of each systems. <span id="S1.F2.8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Relevance</span> measuring context relevance to the query. <span id="S1.F2.8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Recall</span> measuring whether sufficient evidence is covered. </span>(Right)<span id="S1.F2.8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Impact of removing irrelevant triples based on schema frequency on the final performance (LLM-ACC).</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">However, contrary to their theoretical advantages, GraphRAG systems frequently underperform naive RAG systems in many real-world applications <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. This performance decline is primarily due to the low quality of automatically constructed knowledge graphs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Although graph-based retrieval enhances relevant knowledge recall, errors in graph construction introduce substantial noise into the retrieved contexts simultaneously. Fundamentally, these challenges persist because existing pipelines typically derive knowledge from isolated local segments, lacking a global perspective on the previously processed context. This isolation leads to three critical deficiencies that undermine graph quality: (i) <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">thematic irrelevance</span>: extracted triples are often irrelevant to the central theme, introducing meaningless facts.
(ii) <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">logical inconsistency</span>: contradictory facts may emerge within a single subgraph, compromising semantic coherence.
(iii) <span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">structural fragmentation</span>: the built graphs often suffer from fragmentation issues, where the isolated nodes and disconnected components weaken the core advantage of the knowledge graph in supporting global comprehension and multi-hop reasoning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">While some recent studies attempt to improve graph quality before extraction by filtering triples using predefined schema <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sharma et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, these approaches suffer from limited generalization and high manual costs.
Other efforts seek to improve graph quality through bottom-up clustering-based community summarization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Edge et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gutiérrez et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> or topic modeling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sarthi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Nevertheless these unsupervised approaches remain susceptible to error propagation, because inaccuracies in entity relations tend to be amplified at high-level summaries.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To address this, we revisit the pipeline of existing GraphRAG systems and propose a <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">Mem</span>ory-Based Multi-Agent Framework for <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">Graph</span> <span id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">R</span>etrieval-<span id="S1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">A</span>ugmented <span id="S1.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">G</span>eneration (<span id="S1.p5.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MemGraphRAG</span>). Specifically, MemGraphRAG employs a collaborative society of agents supported by a novel Three-Layer
Global Memory. This shared memory structure serves as a unified
knowledge repository, providing a global perspective that enables agents to dynamically coordinate
the extraction process, resolve conflicts upon detection, and integrate fragmented information across
the entire corpus.
To summarize, our contributions are listed as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We identify the root cause of performance degradation in existing GraphRAG systems: the reliance on isolated local extraction. We demonstrate how this lack of global context inevitably leads to three critical deficiencies: thematic irrelevance, logical inconsistency, and structural fragmentation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose MemGraphRAG, which introduces a memory-based multi-agent system into graph construction. The shared memory not only maintains global thematic consistency to prevent irrelevance and fragmentation, but also provides grounded evidence to resolve local logical inconsistencies. Besides, we propose a memory-aware hierarchical retrieval algorithm tailored for the constructed graph.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets, demonstrating that MemGraphRAG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of graph quality, retrieval quality and generation accuracy, validating its practicality for real-world applications.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2. </span>Problem Statement</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To facilitate subsequent discussion, we first introduce key definitions for the knowledge representation, and then present the complete problem formulation of GraphRAG.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1. </span>Key Definitions</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first provide formal definitions for the core components of our knowledge representation:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">(i) <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">type (<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>) and entity (<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>)</span>: a type <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">person</span>) denotes an abstract category, while an entity <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Einstein</span>) is a concrete instance. Formally, a typing function <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> assigns each entity to its specific type, denoted as <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi(e)=t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi(e)=t</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">(ii) <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">schema (<math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>) and fact (<math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>)</span>: a schema <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s=(t_{h},r,t_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s=(t_{h},r,t_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., (<span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">person</span>, <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">born_in</span>, <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">country</span>)) specifies a logical constraint. <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{h},t_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{h},t_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> represent the head and tail types, respectively, <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> denotes a semantic relation. Based on this structure, a fact <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f=(e_{h},r,e_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f=(e_{h},r,e_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., (<span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Einstein</span>, <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">born_in</span>, <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Germany</span>)) is a concrete instantiation of a schema, where <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{h},e_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{h},e_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> represent the head and tail entity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">(iii) <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ontology (<math id="S2.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math>)</span>: the ontology <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as the collection of all valid schemas, denoted as <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}=\{s_{1},\dots,s_{|\mathcal{O}|}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}=\{s_{1},\dots,s_{|\mathcal{O}|}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. It includes the theme and logical rules of the whole knowledge graph.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">(iv) <span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">passage (<math id="S2.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>)</span>: a passage <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the specific text segment acting as the source of the extracted information. We define a function <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi(f)=p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi(f)=p</annotation></semantics></math> to trace each fact <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> back to its origin.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Detailed definitions are provided in Appendix <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2. </span>Problem Formulation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We formally formulate the task of GraphRAG as a unified framework composed of two distinct phases:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">(i) <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Offline Graph Structure Construction</span>. Given a corpus of unstructured documents <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}=\{d_{1},d_{2},...,d_{|\mathcal{D}|}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}=\{d_{1},d_{2},...,d_{|\mathcal{D}|}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, the primary objective is to transform raw text into a structured graph <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})</annotation></semantics></math>. In our framework, the vertex set <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math> is heterogeneous, comprising entities, types, and passages (<math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{V}_{e}\cup\mathcal{V}_{t}\cup\mathcal{V}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{V}_{e}\cup\mathcal{V}_{t}\cup\mathcal{V}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>) , and the edge set <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> encodes the semantic dependencies between them. Formally, this construction process is formalized as</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(1)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\small\mathcal{G}=\texttt{GraphConstructor}(\mathcal{D})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒢</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace" mathsize="0.900em">GraphConstructor</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒟</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\small\mathcal{G}=\texttt{GraphConstructor}(\mathcal{D})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <span id="S2.SS2.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GraphConstructor(*)</span> maps the unstructured corpus to a semantic graph topology, facilitating the efficient navigation from abstract concepts to concrete evidence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">(ii) <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Online Graph-Enhanced Retrieval and Reasoning</span>. Based on the constructed graph <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math>, the system processes a user query <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> to generate a final answer <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>. Unlike extracting isolated text segments, this phase involves identifying optimal reasoning paths within the graph to curate a structured context. The process is formulated as</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(2)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\small a=\texttt{LLM}(\texttt{Retriever}(q,\mathcal{G}))" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">a</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace" mathsize="0.900em">LLM</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace" mathsize="0.900em">Retriever</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒢</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\small a=\texttt{LLM}(\texttt{Retriever}(q,\mathcal{G}))</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <span id="S2.SS2.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Retriever(*)</span> identifies the most relevant graph elements (subgraphs) to support grounded answer generation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.00610v1/pre3.svg" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/257;" width="476" height="257"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>. </span><span id="S2.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Illustration of three conflict types in extracted graphs: 1) Mutually Exclusive Conflict from logically incompatible facts, 2) Temporal Conflict caused by missing temporal grounding for time-varying states, and 3) Granularity Conflict arising from inconsistent abstraction levels for the same entity or concept. Details are in Table <a href="#A3.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix C Details of Preliminary Study ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Details of Preliminary Study ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3. </span>Preliminary Study</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although knowledge graphs can model complex dependencies, recent benchmarks show that advanced GraphRAG systems may underperform naive RAG in real-world QA tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. To investigate this issue, we conduct two preliminary studies to analyze how automatic graph construction affects retrieval quality and downstream generation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1. </span>Performance Degradation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first compare Vanilla RAG with recent GraphRAG systems (MS-GraphRAG, HippoRAG, and GFM-RAG) in the G-Medical dataset<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. As shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(a), GraphRAG methods achieve higher retrieval Recall (e.g., GFM-RAG: 84.3% vs. RAG: 71.8%), but suffer a substantial drop in Relevance (38.5% vs. 62.9%), leading to noisier contexts and lower generation accuracy. These results indicate that existing GraphRAG pipelines often expand the retrieval coverage at the cost of introducing excessive irrelevant information, which ultimately harms the QA performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2. </span>Error Analysis</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further investigate why graph construction introduces noise and conflicts, we hypothesize that the root cause lies in the isolated local extraction paradigm adopted by most baselines. Without a persistent global memory, extraction LLMs process document chunks independently, which leads to systematic issues in graph quality. Specifically, we summarize the major failure modes as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Thematic Irrelevance.</span> Without a global view of the corpus theme, local extraction tends to introduce off-topic triples. To quantify this effect, we conduct a filtering experiment (Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(b)) that removes triples based on schema frequency. Interestingly, filtering out 40% of low-frequency triples slightly improves accuracy (65.28% vs. 64.85%), suggesting that a large fraction of extracted triples are thematically irrelevant noise.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Logical Inconsistency.</span> Independent extraction also introduces semantic contradictions into the merged graph. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.2. Problem Formulation ‣ 2. Problem Statement ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we observe mutually exclusive conflicts, temporal conflicts, and granularity conflicts, which create inconsistent reasoning paths and confuse downstream retrieval. More conflict analyses are provided in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Details of Preliminary Study ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Structural Fragmentation.</span> Due to missing global coreference resolution and schema alignment, key entities are often duplicated or scattered across disconnected subgraphs. This fragmentation prevents effective multi-hop traversal and reduces the usefulness of the graph for global reasoning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3. </span>Discussion</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Current GraphRAG systems exhibit two fundamental limitations. <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">First, existing GraphRAG systems exhibit a fundamental trade-off between recall and relevance.</span> Although graph expansion improves coverage, it often retrieves irrelevant evidence that overwhelms the LLM and degrades generation accuracy. <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Second, current GraphRAG systems lack a global memory mechanism during graph construction.</span> Most systems rely on isolated local extraction, processing document chunks independently without maintaining a persistent global state. As a result, the constructed graph fails to preserve thematic coherence and resolve cross-document conflicts, leading to <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">thematic irrelevance</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">logical inconsistency</span>, and <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">structural fragmentation</span> in downstream retrieval and reasoning processes.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4. </span>Our Framework</h2>

<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.00610v1/framework.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/185;" width="476" height="185" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>. </span><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of the MemGraphRAG framework with two phases: (i) Memory-Based Indexing Graph Construction, where Global Memory (<math id="S4.F4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>) and the Knowledge Graph (<math id="S4.F4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math>) co-evolve via unified schema filtering, global adjudication, and memory-guided bridging; and (ii) Memory-Guided Online Retrieval, which leverages multi-layer memory filtering, structure-aware node initialization, and Personalized PageRank to identify globally relevant contexts for generation.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To overcome fragmented extraction and enable coherent graph evolution, we propose <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MemGraphRAG</span>, a memory-based framework for constructing and maintaining high-quality knowledge graphs. Our key insight is that reliable graph construction requires not only structured storage, but also persistent coordination and correction across documents. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4. Our Framework ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, it consists of two collaborative modules: Memory-based Graph Construction and Memory-guided Retrieval. We first introduce the foundational architecture, followed by the graph construction and retrieval pipelines.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1. </span>MemGraphRAG Architecture</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MemGraphRAG consists of three core components: a <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Global Memory</span> that stores schemas, facts, and passages at different granularities and supports the construction of the <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hierarchical Indexing Graph</span>, and a <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Multi-Agent Group</span> that interacts with memory to iteratively extract, detect, and resolve conflicts. Specifically:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Global Memory (<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>)</span> organizes the extracted knowledge into a three-tier hierarchy, including an <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Ontology Layer</span> (<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{ont}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{ont}</annotation></semantics></math>) that stores schemas with extraction frequencies, a <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Fact Layer</span> (<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math>) that maintains concrete facts, and a <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Passage Layer</span> (<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{pas}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{pas}</annotation></semantics></math>) that preserves original text passages for evidence grounding. To strengthen cross-layer associations, we introduce a <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">dense indexing mechanism</span> that enforces schema consistency and evidence traceability through two bidirectional interactions, where <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">schema-instance alignment</span> links schemas with facts and <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">fact-evidence grounding</span> connects facts with their supporting passages. (See more details in Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2. MemGraphRAG architecture ‣ Appendix D Details of the Proposed Method ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hierarchical Indexing Graph</span> (<math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math>). It provides a unified representation spanning abstract schemas, concrete facts, and textual evidence. It consists of three interconnected graph views: (i) <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Semantic Ontology Graph</span> <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{ont}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{ont}</annotation></semantics></math>, derived from <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{ont}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{ont}</annotation></semantics></math>, which encodes schema-level type relations and structural constraints; (ii) <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Fact Graph</span> <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math>, constructed from <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math>, which represents instantiated entity-relation triples for multi-hop reasoning; and (iii) <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Source Evidence Graph</span> <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{pas}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{pas}</annotation></semantics></math>, induced from <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{pas}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{pas}</annotation></semantics></math>, which grounds facts in <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math> back to their supporting passages. This hierarchical design enables reasoning to traverse from abstract semantics to grounded evidence. More details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2. MemGraphRAG architecture ‣ Appendix D Details of the Proposed Method ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multi-Agent Group</span> (<math id="S4.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>). We introduce a group of agents <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}=\{A_{ext},A_{det},A_{res}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}=\{A_{ext},A_{det},A_{res}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Specifically: (i) the <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Extraction Agent</span> <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{ext}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{ext}</annotation></semantics></math> extracts schemas, facts, and passages into <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math> with evidence grounding; (ii) the <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Conflict Detection Agent</span> <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{det}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{det}</annotation></semantics></math> monitors <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}{fac}</annotation></semantics></math> to detect redundancy, structural anomalies, and logical inconsistencies; and (iii) the <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Conflict Resolution Agent</span> <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A{res}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A{res}</annotation></semantics></math> leverages schema constraints from <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}{ont}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}{ont}</annotation></semantics></math> and historical evidence from <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}{pas}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}{pas}</annotation></semantics></math> to resolve conflicts and maintain global consistency in <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math>. This design separates extraction, diagnosis, and correction for reliable graph construction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2. </span>Memory-based Indexing Graph Construction</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Traditional graph construction often processes document chunks in isolation, resulting in index fragmentation and noise accumulation. To address the critical limitations of <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Thematic Irrelevance</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Logical Inconsistency</span>, and <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Structural Fragmentation</span> identified in our pilot study, we reformulate knowledge graph construction as a dynamic co-evolution process between the Global Memory <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math> and the Knowledge Graph <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math>. Distinct from static extraction pipelines, our approach adheres to three core principles designed to systematically resolve these issues: (i) <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Thematic Denoising via Unified Schema Filtering</span>: Addressing <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Thematic Irrelevance</span>, we employ a unified schema to rigorously filter and manage extracted triples, ensuring that only thematically relevant knowledge is retained; (ii) <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Consistency Maintenance via Global Adjudication</span>: To resolve <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Logical Inconsistency</span>, we utilize the global memory to assist agents in detecting and adjudicating semantic contradictions across disparate documents, thereby ensuring the logical unity of the graph; iii) <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Structural Unification via Memory-Guided Bridging</span>: To overcome <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Structural Fragmentation</span>, we leverage the global memory to identify and merge equivalent entities across disconnected subgraphs. By connecting isolated local extractions and aligning them with the global ontology, we construct a cohesive and interconnected knowledge representation. Specifically, our graph construction procedure is described as follows:</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.1. </span>Thematic Denoising via Unified Schema Filtering</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Graph construction begins with the <span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Extraction Agent</span> <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{ext}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{ext}</annotation></semantics></math>, which transforms each document chunk <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> into structured memory entries. Rather than producing triples alone, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{ext}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{ext}</annotation></semantics></math> jointly constructs entries for all three layers of Global Memory<math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math> by generating candidate schemas, instantiated facts, and their supporting passages:</p>
<table id="S4.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(3)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\small A_{ext}(c_{i})\rightarrow\{\mathcal{S}_{cand}\in\mathcal{M}_{ont},\mathcal{T}_{cand}\in\mathcal{M}_{fac},\mathcal{P}_{src}\in\mathcal{M}_{pas}\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">A</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">c</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em" stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒮</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">d</mi></mrow></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒯</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">d</mi></mrow></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒫</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">c</mi></mrow></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\small A_{ext}(c_{i})\rightarrow\{\mathcal{S}_{cand}\in\mathcal{M}_{ont},\mathcal{T}_{cand}\in\mathcal{M}_{fac},\mathcal{P}_{src}\in\mathcal{M}_{pas}\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This design ensures that each extracted triple is strictly aligned with a schema and grounded in source evidence. To mitigate hallucination accumulation, newly generated schemas are initially treated as candidates and are promoted to stable schemas only when their empirical frequency exceeds a threshold:</p>
<table id="S4.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(4)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\small\mathcal{M}_{ont}^{stable}=\{\,s\in\mathcal{M}_{ont}\mid\mathrm{Freq}(s)\geq\tau\,\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">e</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">Freq</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">≥</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">τ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\small\mathcal{M}_{ont}^{stable}=\{\,s\in\mathcal{M}_{ont}\mid\mathrm{Freq}(s)\geq\tau\,\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Accordingly, only facts aligned with stable schemas are activated for downstream graph construction and reasoning. Detailed extraction procedures are provided in Appendix <a href="#A4.SS3.SSS1" title="D.3.1. Thematic Denoising via Unified Schema Filtering ‣ D.3. Memory-based Indexing Graph Construction ‣ Appendix D Details of the Proposed Method ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.2. </span>Consistency Maintenance via Global Adjudication</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During evolutionary extraction, newly activated triples may introduce redundancy or semantic conflicts with existing facts. To ensure the long-term consistency of the <span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Fact Layer</span> <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math>, We deploy a decoupled diagnosis and correction loop, where the <span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Conflict Detection Agent</span> (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{det}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{det}</annotation></semantics></math>) and the <span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Conflict Resolution Agent</span> (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{res}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{res}</annotation></semantics></math>) collaborate to continuously maintain memory integrity. Specifically, when a new triple <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{new}\in\mathcal{M}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{new}\in\mathcal{M}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math> becomes active, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{det}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{det}</annotation></semantics></math> asynchronously scans existing facts and identifies a conflict set <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{conf}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{conf}</annotation></semantics></math> based on semantic similarity and ontology-level structural constraints:</p>
<table id="S4.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(5)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\small\mathcal{F}_{conf}=\{\,t^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}_{fac}\mid\mathrm{Sim}(t_{new},t^{\prime})&gt;\delta\;\lor\;\mathrm{Match}(t_{new},t^{\prime})\,\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℱ</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">f</mi></mrow></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">′</mo></msup><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">Sim</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">′</mo></msup><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">&gt;</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">δ</mi><mo lspace="0.502em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.502em">∨</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">Match</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">′</mo></msup><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" rspace="0.170em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\small\mathcal{F}_{conf}=\{\,t^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}_{fac}\mid\mathrm{Sim}(t_{new},t^{\prime})&gt;\delta\;\lor\;\mathrm{Match}(t_{new},t^{\prime})\,\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">If <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{conf}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{conf}</annotation></semantics></math> is non-empty, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{res}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{res}</annotation></semantics></math> is triggered to resolve the detected inconsistencies. Rather than generating corrections heuristically, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{res}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{res}</annotation></semantics></math> leverages <span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">fact-evidence grounding</span> to retrieve the provenance passages from <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{pas}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{pas}</annotation></semantics></math> and adjudicates conflicts by comparing the corresponding textual evidence. This evidence-driven resolution enables reliable corrective actions such as filtering invalid facts, merging redundant triples, and resolving temporal or granularity inconsistencies, thereby ensuring that <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math> remains globally coherent throughout the graph construction process.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.3. </span>Structural Unification via Memory-Guided Bridging</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the final phase, we project the refined Global Memory <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math> into the <span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hierarchical Indexing Graph</span> <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math> by constructing three interconnected graph views. Specifically, we build the <span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Semantic Ontology Graph</span> <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{ont}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{ont}</annotation></semantics></math> directly from <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{ont}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{ont}</annotation></semantics></math>, where nodes and edges encode schema-level types and their valid relations, serving as the logical backbone of the overall structure. We then construct the <span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Fact Graph</span> <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math>, where entities form nodes and instantiated triples form edges, enabling multi-hop reasoning over concrete facts. To improve connectivity and reduce fragmentation, we further augment <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math> by introducing additional bridging edges, including type-based connections derived from shared stable schema types in <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{ont}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{ont}</annotation></semantics></math> and similarity-based connections between entities with high embedding similarity. Finally, we induce the <span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Source Evidence Graph</span> <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{pas}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{pas}</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{pas}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{pas}</annotation></semantics></math>, which links facts and entities in <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math> back to their originating passages, ensuring that every reasoning path remains traceable to grounded textual evidence.</p>
</div>

Background colors in <math id="S4.T1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#8FED8F;" mathcolor="#8FED8F" mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.T1.8.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#8FED8F;"> columns</span> represent the magnitude of improvement (Darker green = larger gap).</span></figcaption>

<td id="S4.T1.9.1.25.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.25.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#EBF2FF;">70.30</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.9.1.25.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.25.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#EBF2FF;">69.80</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.9.1.25.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.25.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#EBF2FF;">34.40</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.9.1.25.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.25.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#EBF2FF;">37.90</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.9.1.25.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.25.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#EBF2FF;">68.40</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.9.1.25.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.25.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#EBF2FF;">57.41</span></td>
