<td id="S4.T1.9.1.25.11" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.25.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#EBF2FF;">–</span></td></tr>

<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3. </span>Memory-guided Online Retrieval</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Building upon the Global Hierarchical Graph <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math> and Global Memory <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>, we perform memory-guided retrieval and reasoning in three stages: (i) <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multi-Layer Memory Retrieval</span>, which retrieves candidate schemas, facts, and passages from <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{ont}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{ont}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{pas}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{pas}</annotation></semantics></math>; (ii) <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Structure-Aware Node Initialization</span>, which maps the retrieved evidence to initial node weights based on semantic relevance and structural signals; and (iii) <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Graph Propagation</span>, which runs Personalized PageRank (PPR) over the heterogeneous graph to rank globally important nodes and passages for LLM generation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.1. </span>Multi-Layer Memory Filtering</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The retrieval phase initiates by querying the three distinct layers of the Global Memory<math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math> in parallel. Given a user query <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐪</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{q}</annotation></semantics></math>, we retrieve top-<math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> candidates from <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math> in parallel, including schemas from <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{ont}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{ont}</annotation></semantics></math>, facts from <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math>, and passages from <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{pas}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{pas}</annotation></semantics></math>. To reduce noise before graph reasoning, we retain only schemas and facts whose semantic similarity satisfies <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Sim}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})&gt;\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>Sim</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐪</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Sim}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})&gt;\tau</annotation></semantics></math>. This filtering ensures that subsequent node initialization is seeded with high-confidence structural evidence. If no valid structural candidates remain (i.e., <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}_{ret}\cup\mathcal{F}_{ret}=\emptyset" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}_{ret}\cup\mathcal{F}_{ret}=\emptyset</annotation></semantics></math>), we fall back to standard RAG retrieval by directly selecting passages from <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{pas}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{pas}</annotation></semantics></math> based on query similarity.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.2. </span>Structure-Aware Node Initialization</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To seed graph propagation with query-specific context, we project the retrieved evidence onto the heterogeneous graph by defining an initial reset probability distribution <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{init}(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{init}(v)</annotation></semantics></math> for each node <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\in\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v\in\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math>. This distribution assigns the starting importance of nodes before propagation. We then initialize <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{init}(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{init}(v)</annotation></semantics></math> along three complementary dimensions, as detailed below.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Entity Node Initialization via Facts:</span> To ensure that graph propagation originates from grounded evidence, we initialize each entity node <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math> based on the relevance of its associated retrieved facts. Specifically, its initial weight is defined as the mean similarity over all query-relevant facts containing <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S4.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(6)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\small P_{init}(e)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}_{e}|}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{e}}\mathrm{Sim}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{f})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">P</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">e</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℱ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">e</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" movablelimits="false" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">f</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℱ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">e</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">Sim</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝐪</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝐟</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\small P_{init}(e)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}_{e}|}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{e}}\mathrm{Sim}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{f}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{e}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{ret}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>⊆</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{e}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{ret}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the subset of retrieved facts that contain entity <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>. If <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{e}=\emptyset" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{e}=\emptyset</annotation></semantics></math>, we set <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{init}(e)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{init}(e)=0</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Type Node Initialization via Schemas:</span> We further initialize type nodes <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{schema}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mtext>schema</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{schema}}</annotation></semantics></math> based on the retrieved schemas from <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{\text{ont}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mtext>ont</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{\text{ont}}</annotation></semantics></math> to avoid introducing irrelevant semantics. A critical challenge is that type nodes often exhibit exceptionally large degrees (e.g., a generic “Person” node connected to thousands of entities). Directly activating such high-degree nodes would spread importance across overly many nodes, introducing significant noise. To address this issue, we introduce a structural regularization term that combines semantic relevance with a log-degree penalty:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S4.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(7)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\small P_{init}(t)=\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{t}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\text{Sim}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{s})\right)}_{\text{Schema Relevance}}\times\underbrace{\frac{1}{\log(\text{deg}(t)+1)}}_{\text{Hub Suppression}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">P</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒮</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" movablelimits="false" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒮</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><mtext mathsize="0.900em">Sim</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝐪</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝐬</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext mathsize="0.900em">Schema Relevance</mtext></munder><mo mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mfrac><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext mathsize="0.900em">deg</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext mathsize="0.900em">Hub Suppression</mtext></munder></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\small P_{init}(t)=\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{t}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\text{Sim}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{s})\right)}_{\text{Schema Relevance}}\times\underbrace{\frac{1}{\log(\text{deg}(t)+1)}}_{\text{Hub Suppression}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the retrieved schemas associated with <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. This design incorporates schema-level relevance while preventing overly generic types from dominating propagation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Passage Node Initialization via Information Density:</span> Finally, we initialize the Passage Nodes (<math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in G_{pas}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\in G_{pas}</annotation></semantics></math>) by combining semantic relevance with an information density prior:</p>
<table id="S4.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(8)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\small P_{init}(p)=\text{Sim}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{d}_{p})\times\alpha\times\underbrace{\sigma\left(\frac{\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{p}}\text{IDF}(e)}{\log(|\mathcal{E}_{p}|+1)}\right)}_{\text{Information Density Term}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">P</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext mathsize="0.900em">Sim</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝐪</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝐝</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" rspace="0.055em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">α</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">e</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℰ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext mathsize="0.900em">IDF</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">e</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℰ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">p</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext mathsize="0.900em">Information Density Term</mtext></munder></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\small P_{init}(p)=\text{Sim}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{d}_{p})\times\alpha\times\underbrace{\sigma\left(\frac{\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{p}}\text{IDF}(e)}{\log(|\mathcal{E}_{p}|+1)}\right)}_{\text{Information Density Term}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p6.2" class="ltx_p">This scoring function combines semantic alignment <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Sim}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{d}_{p})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Sim</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐪</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐝</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Sim}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{d}_{p})</annotation></semantics></math>, a dampening factor <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> (set to 0.05) to prevent passage nodes from dominating propagation, and an <span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p6.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Information Density Term</span> that favors passages containing rare and informative entities by aggregating their IDF scores with log-normalization. Detailed initialization procedures are provided in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1. Memory-guided Online Retrieval ‣ Appendix E Prompt Set ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.3. </span>Personalized PageRank</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After initialization, we run Personalized PageRank (PPR) on the heterogeneous graph to propagate query-specific importance. Starting from the normalized distribution <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}^{(0)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}^{(0)}</annotation></semantics></math>, the iteration is defined as <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}^{(k+1)}=(1-\lambda)\mathbf{W}\mathbf{v}^{(k)}+\lambda\mathbf{v}^{(0)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐖𝐯</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}^{(k+1)}=(1-\lambda)\mathbf{W}\mathbf{v}^{(k)}+\lambda\mathbf{v}^{(0)}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the transition matrix and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> is the damping factor. We set <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=0.5</annotation></semantics></math> to limit propagation within a local neighborhood and reduce semantic drift. After convergence, we select the top-<math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> passages and top-<math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> entities ranked by <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}^{(\infty)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}^{(\infty)}</annotation></semantics></math> for LLM inference.</p>
</div>

<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5. </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, our aim is to answer the following questions: <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q1</span> (Generation Accuracy): How does MemGraphRAG perform compared to state-of-the-art GraphRAG methods in terms of generation performance? <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q2</span> (Retrieval Analysis): How does our retrieval method compare to other frameworks in terms of performance and efficiency?<span id="S5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q3</span> (Graph Adaptability Analysis): Can the graph constructed by MemGraphRAG generalize to other GraphRAG methods? <span id="S5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q4</span> (Ablation Study): What contribution does each component of MemGraphRAG make to the overall performance? (Note that additional experiments and case studies are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Additional Experiments ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.)</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1. </span>Experimental Setting</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Datasets.</span> We first evaluate the effectiveness of MemGraphRAG on three widely-used multi-hop QA datasets, including HotpotQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, 2WikiMultiHopQA (2Wiki) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, MuSiQue <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trivedi et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. We follow the settings used in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gutiérrez et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gutiérrez et al., 2025</a>)</cite> for a fair comparison, choosing 1,000 questions from each validation set. We also test our approach on G-Bench(Medical) and G-bench(Novel) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to evaluate MemGraphRAG on complex reasoning across medical, novel knowledge. More details about datasets can be found in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Benchmark Dataset ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baselines.</span> We categorize all baselines into three groups: (i) Zero-shot LLM Inference: We evaluate several foundational models including LLaMA3 (8B) and LLaMA3 (13B)  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dubey et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, as well as GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4o-mini <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2023</a>)</cite>. (ii) We deploy Vanilla RAG across multiple retrieval configurations (retrieving 1, 3, or 5 top passages). (iii) State-of-the-art GraphRAG Systems: We compare against leading GraphRAG implementations, including KGP  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, G-retriever <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, LightRAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, RAPTOR  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sarthi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, MS-GraphRAG<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Edge et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, HippoRAG  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gutiérrez et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gutiérrez et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, GFM-RAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, LazyGRAG<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Darren Edge, 2024</a>)</cite>, E<sup id="S5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_sup">2</sup>GraphRAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, LogicRAG<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025c</a>)</cite> and LinearRAG<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation Metrics.</span> We evaluate our method using four metrics across two categories. For QA performance, following existing work<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we use: 1) String-based accuracy (Str-Acc.), which computes whether the gold answer is included in the generated answer after normalizing them to lowercase words, and 2) LLM-based accuracy (LLM-Acc.), which lets an LLM decide whether the generated answer correctly matches the gold answer. For GraphRAG-bench, since golden answers consist of lengthy descriptive statements, we only evaluate using LLM-ACC. For retrieval quality assessment, we adopt metrics from GraphRAG-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>: 1) <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Context Relevance</span>, which measures semantic alignment between questions and retrieved passages, and 2) <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Evidence Recall</span>, which evaluates whether the retrieved contents contain all the necessary information that used for generating the correct answer.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implementation Details.</span> For consistency, all methods use the same embedding model (<span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, NV-Embed-v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moreira et al., 2024</a>)</cite>). We set <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>=5 for top-<math id="S5.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> retrieval in all methods. For both offline indexing (graph construction) and online generation, we adopt GPT-4o-mini as the default LLM (additional open-source LLM results are reported in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Additional Experiments ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>). For evaluation, we use GPT-4o-mini to compute the LLM-Acc metric. To ensure reproducibility, we set the inference temperature to 0 for all LLM calls.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2. </span>Generation Accuracy (Q1)</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To address Q1, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of generation performance by comparing various baseline methods with MemGraphRAG across four benchmark datasets. The detailed experimental results are presented in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.2.3. Structural Unification via Memory-Guided Bridging ‣ 4.2. Memory-based Indexing Graph Construction ‣ 4. Our Framework ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Based on our analysis, we derive the following key observations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RAG system significantly enhances the LLM generation performance.</span> Direct inference (without retrieval) yields the lowest scores across all benchmarks. For instance, GPT-4o-mini achieves a mere 14.65% average accuracy on MuSiQue in a zero-retrieval setting. Integrating retrieved contexts via Vanilla RAG (top-5) doubles this performance to 30.15%. This confirms that retrieval augmentation is essential for knowledge-intensive tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Graph-based retrieval is more effective for multi-hop reasoning.</span> While increasing the retrieval count (<math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>) improves Vanilla RAG, the performance gains quickly plateau. This limitation stems from Vanilla RAG’s reliance on surface-level keyword matching, which often overlooks the logical bridges required for multi-hop reasoning. In contrast, GraphRAG methods explicitly capture structural dependencies and consistently, and often deliver stronger results. Notably, HippoRAG 2 emerges as a competitive baseline, achieving 38.30% and 56.48% LLM-based accuracy on MuSiQue and G-novel, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MemGraphRAG consistently surpasses existing GraphRAG baselines.</span> While exiting GraphRAGs attempt to align semantics through graph structures, they are often sensitive to noise and low-quality indexing introduced by solated chunk-
level extraction. In contrast, MemGraphRAG mitigates these issues by providing more reliable indexing and retrieval, achieves the best results across all datasets. It reaches 59.25% average accuracy, yielding a 2.10% absolute gain over the strongest baseline.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>. </span><span id="S5.T3.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Adaptability Analysis: MemGraphRAG as a universal graph constructor across different frameworks. The <span id="S5.T3.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#ECF6FF;">blue rows</span> indicate experiments using MemGraphRAG’s constructed graph, while the <span id="S5.T3.6.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F0FF;">purple row</span> represents our full framework. The rightmost column shows the performance gain.</span></figcaption>
<table id="S5.T3.7" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S5.T3.7.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T3.7.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:6.1pt;padding-right:6.1pt;"><span id="S5.T3.7.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GraphConstructor</span></th>
<th id="S5.T3.7.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:6.1pt;padding-right:6.1pt;"><span id="S5.T3.7.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Retriever</span></th>
<th id="S5.T3.7.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:6.1pt;padding-right:6.1pt;"><span id="S5.T3.7.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">HotpotQA</span></th>

<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3. </span>Retrieval Analysis (Q2)</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the retrieval performance of MemGraphRAG, we conducted tests across four distinct task levels on the GraphRAG-Bench. We utilized Recall and Relevance as metrics to assess the GraphRAG’s capacity for retrieving both comprehensive and precise information. Additionally, to assess practical deployment feasibility, we recorded the average retrieval time (in seconds) across all queries. The experimental results are presented in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3.3. Personalized PageRank ‣ 4.3. Memory-guided Online Retrieval ‣ 4. Our Framework ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MemGraphRAG achieves consistently strong retrieval performance, balancing high recall with high relevance.</span> MemGraphRAG consistently ranks at the top in <span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Complex Reasoning</span> tasks (Recall: 90.42, Relevance: 82.64) and <span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Fact Retrieval</span> tasks, significantly outperforming baselines such as HippoRAG2 and LightRAG. These results indicate that our approach effectively filters noise and invalid entity relationships, enabling the system to precisely pinpoint entities and relations relevant to the query. Unlike methods that sacrifice precision for coverage, MemGraphRAG maintains superior relevance while capturing broad context, thereby validating the effectiveness of our <span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Global Adjudication</span> mechanism for consistency maintenance in constructing high-quality graphs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MemGraphRAG achieves the lowest retrieval latency, showing superior online inference efficiency.</span> MemGraphRAG requires an average of only 0.061 seconds per retrieval, which is significantly faster than LightRAG (11.052s) and HippoRAG (1.586s). This efficiency is attributed to our lightweight retrieval process, which relies on efficient Personalized PageRank (PPR) rather than computationally expensive real-time LLM filtering or iterative reasoning loops. Consequently, MemGraphRAG delivers high-precision complex reasoning while maintaining low latency in practice.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4. </span>Indexing Graph Adaptability Analysis (Q3)</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate whether our constructed index graph can seamlessly adapt to different GraphRAG frameworks, we conducted a transferability experiment. Our pilot study previously identified that existing graph construction methods suffer from critical deficiencies, including Thematic Irrelevance, Logical Inconsistency, and Structural Fragmentation. Consequently, we assess whether the structural unification enabled by MemGraphRAG through Memory-Guided Bridging can mitigate these issues for other frameworks. Specifically, we replaced the native graph construction modules of HippoRAG, HippoRAG2, MS-GraphRAG, and LazyGraphRAG with the graph constructed by MemGraphRAG, while retaining their original downstream retrieval and reasoning mechanisms. The comparative experimental results are presented in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.2. Generation Accuracy (Q1) ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.00610v1/ablation.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/232;" width="476" height="232" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>. </span><span id="S5.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Ablation study of MemGraphRAG on three datasets.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MemGraphRAG consistently improves retrieval performance across all evaluated GraphRAG frameworks, serving as a universal high-quality graph constructor.</span> As shown in the results, replacing the original graphs with MemGraphRAG-constructed graphs leads to consistent improvements for all baseline retrievers across all datasets. For instance, the average performance of HippoRAG increases from 51.07 to 51.78, and MS-GraphRAG improves from 43.75 to 44.21. This consistent improvement shows that our memory-driven global construction mechanism effectively mitigates structural fragmentation and logical inconsistencies. By producing a more cohesive and thematically aligned knowledge structure, MemGraphRAG substantially strengthens the effectiveness of existing retrievers, demonstrating its robustness as a foundational indexing solution.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5. </span>Ablation Study (Q4)</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To verify the contribution of each module in MemGraphRAG, we conduct an ablation study on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and G-Medical. We compare the full model with four variants that remove the <span id="S5.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Schema Filter</span>, <span id="S5.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Conflict Resolution</span>, <span id="S5.SS5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hub Suppression</span>, and the <span id="S5.SS5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Information Density Term</span>, respectively. As shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 5.4. Indexing Graph Adaptability Analysis (Q3) ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, MemGraphRAG consistently achieves the best performance across all datasets (e.g., 69.40% on HotpotQA), which indicates that these memory-driven graph construction and initialization mechanisms are jointly crucial for building a robust knowledge graph.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">w/o Schema Filter:</span> Removing <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Unified Schema Filtering</span> causes a clear degradation, especially on 2WikiMultiHopQA and G-Medical (68.10% and 65.92%). Without the frequency-based stability constraint (<math id="S5.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Freq}(s)\geq\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>Freq</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Freq}(s)\geq\tau</annotation></semantics></math>), low-frequency and off-topic schemas are retained, introducing noisy triples that weaken semantic focus.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">w/o Conflict Resolution:</span> Excluding <span id="S5.SS5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Global Adjudication</span> leads to the largest drop on HotpotQA (66.95%). Without conflict detection and resolution, the fact layer accumulates contradictory or redundant triples, which disrupts multi-hop reasoning chains and increases the chance of retrieving inconsistent evidence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">w/o Hub Suppression:</span> Removing <span id="S5.SS5.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hub Suppression</span> reduces accuracy (67.22% on HotpotQA). Without degree-based regularization, generic high-degree nodes dominate propagation, causing semantic drift toward irrelevant subgraphs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">w/o Information Density Term:</span> Dropping the <span id="S5.SS5.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Information Density Term</span> yields a smaller but consistent decline (68.67% on HotpotQA). Without IDF-style weighting, passage initialization cannot prioritize discriminative evidence, weakening the model’s ability to anchor reasoning on informative documents.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6. </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we propose MemGraphRAG, a novel GraphRAG framework that integrates a global memory mechanism into the knowledge graph construction process. By leveraging a shared hierarchical memory structure, our multi-agent system collaboratively maintains a global perspective throughout both the extraction and retrieval phases. This paradigm effectively overcomes key limitations of traditional GraphRAG approaches that rely on isolated local extraction. It systematically mitigates thematic irrelevance, logical inconsistency, and structural fragmentation, thereby enabling a globally consistent indexing graph. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MemGraphRAG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of graph quality, retrieval precision, and generation accuracy, providing a robust solution for deploying reliable RAG systems in complex real-world scenarios.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Limitation</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While MemGraphRAG demonstrates strong robustness in processing large-scale textual corpora and constructing globally consistent knowledge graphs, its current design is limited to unimodal textual inputs. However, real-world knowledge repositories are inherently multimodal, containing heterogeneous formats such as statistical charts, technical diagrams, document layouts, and embedded images in academic papers or financial reports. Currently, our framework requires non-textual elements to be transcribed or described in text before processing, which may lead to the loss of critical visual semantics and spatial relationships. For example, quantitative trends in line charts or complex structures in scientific diagrams often contain dense information that textual descriptions cannot fully capture, potentially causing information loss during indexing. Extending the <span id="Sx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Global Hierarchical Graph</span> to incorporate multimodal nodes (e.g., embedding visual patches into the <span id="Sx1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Fact Layer</span> <math id="Sx1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math> or the <span id="Sx1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Passage Layer</span> <math id="Sx1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{pas}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{pas}</annotation></semantics></math>) is a promising direction for future work. Such an extension could enable cross-modal reasoning, allowing the multi-agent system to verify textual claims against visual evidence and further improve the versatility of MemGraphRAG.</p>
</div>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Additional Experiments</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1. </span>Ablation on Backbone LLMs</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further evaluate the universality and robustness of MemGraphRAG, we conducted experiments utilizing the stronger <span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">llama-3-70b- instruct</span> as the underlying backbone model. We compared our method against a comprehensive suite of baselines, ranging from non-structured methods (e.g., Vanilla RAG) to state-of-the-art graph-based approaches (e.g., HippoRAG2, E2GraphRAG). The results are detailed in Table <a href="#A1.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ A.1. Ablation on Backbone LLMs ‣ Appendix A Additional Experiments ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MemGraphRAG consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated datasets, highlighting its compatibility and robustness across different backbone models.</span> As shown in the table, MemGraphRAG achieves the highest average performance of 58.41%, significantly outperforming the strongest baseline, HippoRAG2 (55.41%), and surpassing standard graph-based methods like LightRAG (47.81%) by a substantial margin. First, compared to non-structured methods, our approach exhibits a dominant advantage over Vanilla RAG (Top-5 average: 47.52%), validating that our memory-driven graph structure effectively captures long-range dependencies that vector retrieval misses. Second, in the realm of graph-based RAG, MemGraphRAG excels particularly in multi-hop reasoning tasks. On the 2WikiMultiHopQA dataset, we achieve a Containment Accuracy of 69.40% and an LLM Accuracy of 66.80%, notably higher than HippoRAG2 (61.90% and 54.40%, respectively). This indicates that our method constructs a more connected and logically coherent graph, enabling the retriever to accurately locate multi-hop evidence chains. Furthermore, on domain-specific datasets like G-Medical, MemGraphRAG maintains its lead (67.13%), proving its robustness in handling specialized knowledge. Collectively, these results confirm that MemGraphRAG provides a high-quality, globally consistent indexing structure that universally enhances the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A1.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>. </span><span id="A1.T4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of different methods. The column <math id="A1.T4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> shows the improvement of <span id="A1.T4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MemGraphRAG</span> (58.41) over baselines. Darker green in <math id="A1.T4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> indicates a larger performance gap.</span></figcaption>
<div id="A1.T4.6" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:108.5pt;vertical-align:-53.0pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-175.9pt,55.3pt) scale(0.495086538849366,0.495086538849366) ;">
<table id="A1.T4.6.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A1.T4.6.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T4.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" rowspan="2"><span id="A1.T4.6.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Method</span></th>

<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2. </span>Graph Analysis</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To more intuitively assess the quality of the index graphs produced by our memory-based construction approach, we analyze their topological properties and compare MemGraphRAG with existing baselines in terms of connectivity, redundancy, and semantic aggregation. Following previous study <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we assessed the Average Degree and Average Clustering Coefficient of the index graphs constructed by various GraphRAG frameworks on the G-Medical and G-Novel datasets. The comparative results are presented in Table <a href="#A1.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ A.2. Graph Analysis ‣ Appendix A Additional Experiments ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and Figure <a href="#A1.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ A.2. Graph Analysis ‣ Appendix A Additional Experiments ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MemGraphRAG demonstrates superior entity-level connectivity compared to existing GraphRAG methods.</span> MemGraphRAG achieves the highest Average Degree on both datasets, reaching 14.37 on the Medical dataset (surpassing HippoRAG2’s 13.31) and 9.26 on the Novel dataset (surpassing HippoRAG2’s 8.75). This improvement indicates that our memory consistency maintenance mechanism effectively links entities scattered across different document chunks. As a result, it bridges fragmented subgraphs and enables more robust long-range reasoning paths.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MemGraphRAG demonstrates superior subgraph-level semantic clustering than existing GraphRAG methods.</span> MemGraphRAG also attains the highest Average Clustering Coefficients, with 0.865 on the G-Novel and 0.527 on the G-Medical. These results indicate that nodes in MemGraphRAG tend to share common neighbors, leading to denser local connectivity and clearer semantic clusters. This further shows that MemGraphRAG integrates dispersed knowledge into a more unified and highly structured index graph, instead of yielding sparse graphs composed of loosely related facts.</p>
</div>

<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3. </span>Case Study</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct a qualitative analysis in Table <a href="#A1.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ A.3. Case Study ‣ Appendix A Additional Experiments ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> and Table <a href="#A1.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ A.3. Case Study ‣ Appendix A Additional Experiments ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> to illustrate how MemGraphRAG overcomes the limitations of isolated extraction by ensuring logical consistency and thematic purity through its global memory mechanism.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">1) <span id="A1.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Case Study on Conflict Resolution.</span> Table <a href="#A1.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ A.3. Case Study ‣ Appendix A Additional Experiments ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> illustrates a representative scenario of Mutually Exclusive Conflict, where disparate documents claim conflicting birth years for the same entity ("1645" vs. "1643"). Traditional pipelines simply aggregate these contradictions, leading to ambiguous reasoning paths. MemGraphRAG addresses this through Global Adjudication. Upon detecting the conflict, the Resolution Agent (<math id="A1.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{res}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{res}</annotation></semantics></math>) retrieves the original provenance from the Passage Layer (<math id="A1.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{pas}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{pas}</annotation></semantics></math>) and validates the correct fact ("1643") before indexing. This mechanism effectively eliminates logical incoherence, enabling the retriever to provide an accurate context for the LLM.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">2) <span id="A1.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Case Study on Thematic Denoising.</span> In domain-specific tasks (e.g., medical protocols), LLMs often extract irrelevant noise alongside core facts. As shown in Table <a href="#A1.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ A.3. Case Study ‣ Appendix A Additional Experiments ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, the baseline graph is polluted by irrelevant triples (e.g., Patient prefers Tea), which distracts the retrieval process. MemGraphRAG mitigates this via Unified Schema Filtering. By treating extracted schemas as candidate and only stabilizing those that exceed a frequency threshold (<math id="A1.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>), our system successfully filters out irrelevant noise while retaining stable clinical patterns (e.g., <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Drug\xrightarrow{treats}Disease" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mover accent="true"><mo>→</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">s</mi></mrow></mover><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Drug\xrightarrow{treats}Disease</annotation></semantics></math>). This results in a cleaner Fact Graph (<math id="A1.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{fac}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{fac}</annotation></semantics></math>) that strictly follows the domain ontology, significantly improving retrieval precision.</p>
</div>

<td id="A1.T6.5.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" colspan="2"><span id="A1.T6.5.4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Q: “When was Isaac Newton born?”</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T6.5.5" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T6.5.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="A1.T6.5.5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">4. Retrieval Process</span></th>
<td id="A1.T6.5.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">

</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1. </span>Retrieval-Augmented Generation</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities, they remain prone to hallucination <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2026b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates this by grounding generation in external evidence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guu et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Borgeaud et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Izacard et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. However, effectively organizing fragmented knowledge from distributed documents to support complex reasoning remains a persistent challenge.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address this, recent research has evolved from simple retrieval to Reasoning-enhanced RAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Asai et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Departing from static index construction, this paradigm focuses on interleaving the retrieval process with the logical flow of the LLM. Several approaches optimize the retrieval process through Chain-of-Thought prompting, recursive inner monologues, or logical decomposition, such as IRCoT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trivedi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, IM-RAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and LAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. LogicRAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025c</a>)</cite> advances this direction by eliminating pre-built graphs entirely, instead constructing a reasoning Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) dynamically at inference time to enable adaptive retrieval planning. While effective, these methods typically operate within the constraints of fixed resources or rely on the LLM’s inherent reasoning capabilities rather than structured knowledge representation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2. </span>Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To overcome the limitations of unstructured text chunks, GraphRAG focuses on explicit graph structure construction to capture global dependencies and structural patterns. Current approaches can be categorized into two primary construction paradigms:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Relation-extraction-based Construction.</span> This line of work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gutiérrez et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gusarov et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luo et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tsang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025c</a>)</cite> structures text corpora into Knowledge Graphs (KGs) by extracting triples to form atomic knowledge units. These units are subsequently unified via entity alignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, enabling the application of sophisticated graph reasoning algorithms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qu and Tang, 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">LUO et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Some methods augment reasoning by integrating these static KGs as navigational aids, such as Think-on-Graph <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and RRP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>. However, independent OpenIE extraction often leads to inconsistency. Although schema-guided approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sharma et al., 2024</a>)</cite> attempt to standardize this, they entail high manual costs. Addressing these inefficiencies, LinearRAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> proposes a relation-free “Tri-Graph” based on lightweight entity extraction, achieving linear scalability without the noise associated with traditional triple extraction.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Clustering-based Hierarchy Construction.</span> Complementary to triple-based methods, this category focuses on capturing global information by identifying dense structural patterns. Methods typically employ community detection algorithms, such as Louvain or Leiden, to recursively aggregate entities into clusters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Edge et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sarthi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gutiérrez et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. These clusters serve as hierarchical summaries, abstracting raw passages into topic-level communities to provide a macro-level perspective. Despite its utility in summarizing high-level themes, this unsupervised approach faces limitations regarding precision, as inaccuracies in low-level entity relationships can propagate upward, and the iterative clustering of large-scale graphs poses significant bottlenecks for real-time deployment.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Details of Preliminary Study</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Independent extraction across different chunks may introduce conflicting information into the merged graph, resulting in semantic contradictions. In our preliminary study, we identify three major types of such conflicts, as summarized in Table <a href="#A3.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix C Details of Preliminary Study ‣ MemGraphRAG: Memory-based Multi-Agent System for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>. Specifically:</p>
<ul id="A3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mutually Exclusive Conflict:</span> Facts that cannot coexist in reality. For example, Chunk A yields <span id="A3.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Newton, Birth year, 1643)</span> while Chunk B yields <span id="A3.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Newton, Birth year, 1645)</span>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Temporal Conflict:</span> Contradictions arising from time-variant facts. A corpus spanning different years may generate both <span id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Biden, President, USA)</span> and <span id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Trump, President, USA)</span> without temporal qualifiers, confusing the retriever.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Granularity Conflict:</span> Facts describing the same reality at incompatible abstraction levels. For instance, connecting an entity to both specific and general concepts, such as <span id="A3.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Xiao Ming, born_in, Shanghai)</span> and <span id="A3.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Xiao Ming, born_in, China)</span>, or <span id="A3.I1.i3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(AI, subclass, NLP)</span> vs. <span id="A3.I1.i3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(AI, subclass, Unsupervised Learning)</span>. These inconsistencies create redundant paths that dilute the reasoning focus.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T8" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A3.T8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 8</span>. </span><span id="A3.T8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Taxonomy of Knowledge Conflicts in Graph Retrieval-Augmented Systems.</span></figcaption>

<tr id="A3.T8.5.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A3.T8.5.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;">
<span id="A3.T8.5.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:85.4pt;">
